chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Arranging for Tiny Hill: road trips and listening to the band first
summary: Horace rode with Tiny to dates in Mounds, Illinois, heard the band several times and noted each man's role before writing, keeping Tiny's vocals uncluttered.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And so we used to sit down and talk these things over, even before I made the arrangements, you know. I said, 'Well, I don't want to get far out,' you know. And I said, 'How do you want this,' one of these things, and I -- he would leave it to my discretion. He says, 'I tell you what you do.' He says, 'Why don't you come down. I'm playing at a little town called Mounds, Illinois, way down in the southern part of Illinois, you know. He says -- naturally, he paid for the transportation and things coming down there, and he wasn't cheap or anything, about it. And they used to travel in cars, and whatnot. And Tiny had a special seat, naturally, big as he was, you know. And he'd have little compartments over there, little nips and (unintelligible) things like that.
: He was just all organized, huh?
You know -- and we'd talk and we'd just go down the highway, and we'd tell jokes, and we would

get the biggest kick out of some things I'd tell him, you know, about what had happened in Fletcher's band, you know, like the things Hawk and those guys used to do. And, man, he'd crack up. He said, "You got to tell this to my guys."

And we would get in town and the band was never late. He was strict that way, and they knew Tiny. And we used to have an hour and a half a lot of times in the towns, and we kept in the background, the dressing room, and the guys would just have a ball and talk those things, and it was a (unintelligible) and all, and in this particular town like Mounds, Illinois, he'd have me come to hear the band, you know, a lot. In fact, I think I heard the band three or four times before I ventured to do any writing. I got so I would know the individuals and their capabilities quite well before I would write anything, see, and I would take my little book and write down, "this guy -- solo; this guy -- no solo, straight, you know and all that stuff. "Tenor man, vocalists and all that, stuff. (Unintelligible) and all of that. And it made it easier to write after I'd heard them, you know. And then I made a couple of things with Tiny singing, and I knew how he liked to sing, and how he liked so many fill ins, and he didn't like anything, you know, [movements] to get in his way. I remember this and all, you know. So it was easy. So we just did fine. And we became

friends over a period of years, even when he became ill. He was out in Iowa somewhere here, oh, a year and a half ago, and he was connected in some other profession, and I used to get letters from him. He'd always send me little quotes and things, you know.
